title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
caption: Extensor Digitorum Longus Patient Position The patient is positioned supine or in supported long sitting with the knee slightly flexed and the anterior ankle exposed. The foot is supported in a comfortable position with slight plantar flexion as tolerated. This position provides access to the superficial extensor tendons while allowing movement of the ankle and toes during dynamic assessment. Sufficient ultrasound gel and light transducer pressure help maintain contact without compressing the superficial tendon sheath. Figure 1A: Long Axis (LAX) Transducer Placement The LAX view is obtained by positioning the transducer over the anterior ankle, parallel to the extensor digitorum longus tendon fibers. First identify the tendon in a transverse survey, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus, and then rotate the transducer to follow its longitudinal course. The distal tibia and talus provide deep bony landmarks as the tendon crosses the ankle. Trace the tendon proximally toward the musculotendinous junction and distally toward its divisions on the dorsum of the foot. Active extension of the second through fifth toes helps confirm extensor digitorum longus identification by demonstrating tendon excursion. Figures 1B–1D: Short Axis (SAX) Transducer Placement (Muscle Belly, Anterior Ankle, Dorsal Foot) The SAX view is obtained by rotating the transducer 90 degrees from the LAX position, placing it perpendicular to the tendon fibers. At the anterior ankle, identify the tibialis anterior tendon medially, the extensor hallucis longus tendon centrally, and the extensor digitorum longus tendons laterally. Translate the transducer proximally and distally to assess tendon size, internal echogenicity, and the surrounding sheath. Extension of the second through fifth toes helps distinguish extensor digitorum longus excursion from that of the neighboring extensor hallucis longus during great-toe extension.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
caption: NORMAL VIEW IN LONG AXIS (LAX) Figures 2A and 2B: Long Axis View In the LAX view, the extensor digitorum longus tendon appears as a continuous, hyperechoic fibrillar structure crossing superficial to the anterior ankle joint. The distal tibial and talar cortices form bright interfaces deep to the tendon and joint capsule. Normal tendon fibers maintain a uniform, parallel arrangement without focal thickening or disruption. Minimal to no fluid should be visible within the tendon sheath. Small heel-to-toe transducer adjustments may be necessary to reduce anisotropy, particularly where the tendon changes direction across the ankle. Dynamic extension of the second through fifth toes should demonstrate smooth tendon excursion.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
caption: NORMAL VIEW IN SHORT AXIS (SAX) Figures 3A–3F: SAX View (3A/3B Muscle Belly, 3C/3D Talus, 3E/3F Midfoot) In the SAX, the extensor digitorum longus can be followed from its muscle belly in the anterior compartment of the leg across the anterior ankle and onto the dorsum of the foot. Proximally, the muscle belly lies adjacent to the fibula and superficial to the extensor hallucis longus, displaying hypoechoic muscle fascicles separated by echogenic connective tissue. At the anterior ankle, the extensor digitorum longus tendons appear as echogenic oval or rounded structures with a finely stippled internal pattern within a common tendon sheath. They lie lateral to the extensor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior tendons and superficial to the anterior joint capsule, with the bright cortical reflection of the talus providing a deep bony landmark. Further distally over the cuneiforms, the individual tendon slips become more distinctly separated, coursing superficial to the intrinsic extensor musculature and dorsal capsuloligamentous structures toward the second through fifth toes. Throughout the examination, tendon contours should remain well defined, without focal enlargement or surrounding sheath distention. Adjust the transducer angle as the tendons change course to maintain perpendicular insonation and minimize anisotropy.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
caption: EXTENSOR DIGITORUM LONGUS TENOSYNOVITIS Figures 4A (LAX) and 4B (SAX): Extensor Digitorum Longus Tenosynovitis The supplied images demonstrate fluid distending the extensor digitorum tendon sheath in both LAX and SAX. In the LAX view, hypoechoic to anechoic fluid extends alongside the echogenic tendon fibers. In the SAX view, fluid outlines portions of the tendon cross sections, making the expanded sheath more apparent. These findings are compatible with tenosynovitis in the appropriate clinical setting. Tendon fiber continuity should be assessed separately to determine whether associated tendon injury is present.

label: FIGURE 4
caption: Patient 2. Volar wrist HADD; intraosseous migration. Imaging correlation. (A) Conventional radiography obtained 3 days after the acute onset of atraumatic volar wrist pain, in a 45‐year‐old woman, demonstrates calcific deposits along the volar side of the wrist. (B) Longitudinal sonogram at the volar radiocarpal joint (radio‐scaphoid) obtained the same day. Note the calcific deposit along the wrist capsule (black arrowhead). Anteriorly, a second deposit is near the scaphoid, which shows a discontinuity (curved arrow) where the calcium migrated intraosseous (open arrowhead). There are edematous changes of the neighboring tissue (asterisk), appearing diffusely hyperechoic. (C) Corresponding sagittal CT obtained 10 days later confirms the calcific deposit (black arrowhead) as well as the mild bony irregularity related to the intraosseous migration. (D) MRI obtained 1 week after the CT study. The deposit is difficult to demonstrate. Note the edema (asterisk) in the region where US and CT show the calcium deposit, near the flexor carpi radialis (fcr, partially shown) and the small subcortical erosion on the scaphoid distal pole (curved arrow) with associated mild bone marrow edema. Rest and NSAIDs were suggested with progressive clinical improvement at one and 3 months. A final diagnosis of acute periarticular inflammation due to HADD of the volar wrist capsule, with concomitant CTS was proposed.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Carpal Tunnel and Median Nerve
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
label: Figures 2A and 2B.
caption: SAX of Median Nerve at the Carpal Tunnel Inlet When performing a SAX view in ultrasound, Figure 1B , it is often helpful to begin by identifying key bony acoustic landmarks. In this case, start by locating the carpal tunnel inlet after visualizing the median nerve. The median nerve is distinguished by its characteristic honeycomb appearance, displaying darker fascicles interspersed with connective tissue. This architecture contrasts with the surrounding flexor tendons, which exhibit a finer, more fibular texture. To further differentiate the median nerve from nearby structures, we utilize a technique called toggling the transducer allowing for a subtle rocking motion. Tendons are anisotropic, meaning their echogenicity changes with the angle of insonation; they may appear brighter or darker as the transducer angle shifts. In contrast, the median nerve maintains a more consistent appearance regardless of angle, aiding in its identification. At the carpal tunnel inlet, we observe the rounded dome of the pisiform on the ulnar side and the curved surface of the scaphoid on the radial side. This is commonly the region where the median nerve shows its greatest cross-sectional area. The transverse carpal ligament forms the roof of the tunnel at this level. Adjacent to the pisiform, we also see the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery, which course through the ulnar tunnel (Guyon’s canal). This canal is formed by the floor of the transverse carpal ligament and contains these neurovascular structures.

In this view, the median nerve appears superficial, lying above the flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus tendons. The median nerve is easily recognized by its fascicular architecture, which remains distinct in this orientation. This scanning plane provides a clear view of the carpal tunnel space, and you may gently mobilize the flexor tendons to observe their movement. While both the tendons and the median nerve exhibit excursion during finger motion, the median nerve displays less excursion compared to the tendons beneath it. This dynamic observation is a helpful method for evaluating median nerve mobility and for identifying structures within the carpal tunnel.

caption: SAX View of Median Nerve in the Carpal Tunnel Ultrasound features of carpal tunnel syndrome include a hypoechoic, thickened median nerve with loss of the normal “honeycomb” fascicular pattern. Cross-sectional area thresholds aid diagnosis: <8 mm² is normal, 8–12 mm² is borderline, and >12 mm² is abnormal. A CSA increase of >2 mm² from the forearm (pronator quadratus level) to the wrist carpal tunnel is 100% specific for carpal tunnel syndrome. In Figure 5A, the circumference measures 10 mm².

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Carpal Tunnel and Median Nerve
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
label: Figure 6A.
caption: LAX View of Median Nerve in the Carpal Tunnel. In diagnostic ultrasound of the median nerve at the wrist, the “notch sign” highlighted above with the yellow arrow refers to a key finding observed in the LAX view in cases of carpal tunnel syndrome. As the median nerve approaches the proximal carpal tunnel, it typically appears thickened and hypoechoic, reflecting early swelling due to compression. At the level of the flexor retinaculum, the nerve then abruptly flattens, creating a distinct “notch” or step-off in its contour. This change in shape of being thickened proximally and flattened distally is known as the notch sign and is a hallmark of median nerve entrapment at the carpal tunnel inlet. This finding is often seen in conjunction with other sonographic features such as volar bowing of the flexor retinaculum and an increased cross-sectional area of the median nerve in the transverse view. The notch sign provides visual confirmation of mechanical compression and supports the clinical diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.
